{{Short description|Munchausen number}}
In [[number theory]], a '''perfect digit-to-digit invariant''' ('''PDDI'''; also known as a '''Munchausen number'''<ref name="curious">{{cite arXiv|last=van Berkel|first=Daan|title=On a curious property of 3435|year=2009|eprint=0911.3038|class=math.HO }}</ref>) is a [[natural number]] in a given [[number base]] <math>b</math> that is equal to the sum of its digits each raised to the power of itself. An example in base 10 is 3435, because <math>3435 = 3^3 + 4^4 + 3^3 + 5^5</math>. The term "Munchausen number" was coined by Dutch mathematician and software engineer Daan van Berkel in 2009,<ref>Olry, Regis and Duane E. Haines. [https://books.google.com/books?id=h30pAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA136 "Historical and Literary Roots of Münchhausen Syndromes"], from Literature, Neurology, and Neuroscience: Neurological and Psychiatric Disorders, Stanley Finger, Francois Boller, Anne Stiles, eds. Elsevier, 2013. p.136.</ref> as this evokes the story of [[Baron Munchausen]] raising himself up by his own ponytail because each digit is raised to the power of itself.<ref name=dvb>Daan van Berkel,  [https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.3038 ''On a curious property of 3435.'']</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Parker|first1=Matt|title=Things to Make and Do in the Fourth Dimension|date=2014|publisher=Penguin UK|isbn=9781846147654|page=28|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AOu2AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT28|access-date=2 May 2015}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>n</math> be a natural number which can be written in base <math>b</math> as the k-digit number <math>d_{k-1}d_{k-2}...d_{1}d_{0}</math> where each digit <math>d_i</math> is between <math>0</math> and <math>b-1</math> inclusive, and <math>n = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} d_{i}b^{i}</math>. We define the function <math>F_b : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}</math> as <math>F_b(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k - 1} {d_i}^{d_i}</math>. (As [[0 to the power of 0|0<sup>0</sup>]] is usually undefined, there are typically two conventions used, one where it is taken to be equal to one, and another where it is taken to be equal to zero.<ref>[http://www.magic-squares.net/narciss.htm Narcisstic Number], Harvey Heinz</ref><ref>{{cite book 
  | last = Wells 
  | first = David 
  | title = The Penguin Dictionary of Curious and Interesting Numbers 
  | publisher = Penguin 
  | location = London 
  | year = 1997 
  | page = 185 
  | isbn = 0-14-026149-4}}</ref>) A natural number <math>n</math> is defined to be a perfect digit-to-digit invariant in base b if <math>F_b(n) = n</math>. For example, the number 3435 is a perfect digit-to-digit invariant in base 10 because <math>3^3 + 4^4 + 3^3 + 5^5 = 27 + 256 + 27 + 3125 = 3435</math>. 

<math>F_b(1) = 1</math> for all <math>b</math>, and thus 1 is a ''trivial'' perfect digit-to-digit invariant in all bases, and all other perfect digit-to-digit invariants are ''nontrivial''. For the second convention where <math>0^0 = 0</math>, both <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> are trivial perfect digit-to-digit invariants.

A natural number <math>n</math> is a ''sociable'' digit-to-digit invariant if it is a [[periodic point]] for <math>F_{b}</math>, where <math>F_{b}^k(n) = n</math> for a positive integer <math>k</math>, and forms a [[Periodic sequence|cycle]] of period <math>k</math>. A perfect digit-to-digit invariant is a sociable digit-to-digit invariant with <math>k = 1</math>. An ''amicable'' digit-to-digit invariant is a sociable digit-to-digit invariant with <math>k = 2</math>.

All natural numbers <math>n</math> are [[periodic point#iterated function|preperiodic points]] for <math>F_b</math>, regardless of the base. This is because all natural numbers of base <math>b</math> with <math>k</math> digits satisfy <math>b^{k-1} \leq n \leq (k){(b - 1)}^{b-1}</math>. However, when <math>k \geq b+1</math>, then <math>b^{k-1} > (k){(b - 1)}^{b-1}</math>, so any <math>n</math> will satisfy <math>n > F_b(n)</math> until <math>n < b^{b+1}</math>. There are a finite number of natural numbers less than <math>b^{b+1}</math>, so the number is guaranteed to reach a periodic point or a fixed point less than <math>b^{b+1}</math>, making it a preperiodic point. This means also that there are a finite number of perfect digit-to-digit invariant and [[Periodic sequence|cycles]] for any given base <math>b</math>.

The number of iterations <math>i</math> needed for <math>F_b^{i}(n)</math> to reach a fixed point is the <math>b</math>-factorion function's [[persistence of a number|persistence]] of <math>n</math>, and undefined if it never reaches a fixed point.

==Programming examples==

The following program in [[Python (programming language)|Python]] determines whether an [[Integer (computer science)|integer]] number is a Munchausen Number / Perfect Digit to Digit Invariant or not, following the convention <math>0^0 = 1</math>.
<syntaxhighlight lang="python3">
num = int(input("Enter number:"))
temp = num
s = 0.0
while num > 0:
     digit = num % 10
     num //= 10
     s+= pow(digit, digit)
     
if s == temp:
    print("Munchausen Number")
else:
    print("Not Munchausen Number")
</syntaxhighlight>

The examples below implement the perfect digit-to-digit invariant function described in the definition above [[Cycle detection|to search for perfect digit-to-digit invariants and cycles]] in [[Python (programming language)|Python]] for the two conventions.

=== Convention 0<sup>0</sup> = 1 ===
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def pddif(x: int, b: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    while x > 0:
        total = total + pow(x % b, x % b)
        x = x // b
    return total

def pddif_cycle(x: int, b: int) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    while x not in seen:
        seen.append(x)
        x = pddif(x, b)
    cycle = []
    while x not in cycle:
        cycle.append(x)
        x = pddif(x, b)
    return cycle
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Convention 0<sup>0</sup> = 0 ===
<syntaxhighlight lang="python" start="0">
def pddif(x: int, b: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    while x > 0:
        if x % b > 0:
            total = total + pow(x % b, x % b)
        x = x // b
    return total

def pddif_cycle(x: int, b: int) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    while x not in seen:
        seen.append(x)
        x = pddif(x, b)
    cycle = []
    while x not in cycle:
        cycle.append(x)
        x = pddif(x, b)
    return cycle
</syntaxhighlight>
